title: Physics: An Introduction
lead: Physics describes the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and a surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe. You will meet the realm of physics and its applications, what scientists mean by a model, a theory, and a law, and how experiment decides between them. Classical physics is an excellent approximation under stated conditions, and relativity and quantum mechanics make up modern physics.
objectives: Explain the difference between a principle and a law.
Explain the difference between a model and a theory.
summary_html:
• Science seeks to discover and describe the underlying order and simplicity in nature.
  • Physics is the most basic of the sciences, concerning itself with energy, matter, space and time, and their interactions.
  • Scientific laws and theories express the general truths of nature and the body of knowledge they encompass. These laws of nature are rules that all natural processes appear to follow.

figures.original_caption: What is a model? This planetary model of the atom shows electrons orbiting the nucleus. It is a drawing that we use to form a mental image of the atom that we cannot see directly with our eyes because it is too small.

exercises.prompt: A friend tells you they have learned about a new law of nature. What can you know about the information even before your friend describes the law? How would the information be different if your friend told you they had learned about a scientific theory rather than a law?

answer.solution: Without knowing the details of the law, you can still infer that the information your friend has learned conforms to the requirements of all laws of nature: it will be a concise description of the universe around us; a statement of the underlying rules that all natural processes follow. If the information had been a theory, you would be able to infer that the information will be a large-scale, broadly applicable generalization.

exercises.prompt: Models are particularly useful in relativity and quantum mechanics, where conditions are outside those normally encountered by humans. What is a model?

answer.solution: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult, or impossible, to display directly. Experimental proof justifies a model, but it is accurate only under limited situations, and it describes certain aspects of a physical system rather than all of them. The planetary model of the atom is the text’s example. We cannot observe electron orbits, but the mental image of electrons going round a nucleus helps explain the observations we can make, such as the light given off by hot gases. That is why models matter so much in relativity and quantum mechanics: we never experience those phenomena directly, and a picture we can relate to in human terms is the way in to them.

exercises.prompt: How does a model differ from a theory?

answer.solution: A model is a picture of something we cannot see directly, and it describes only certain aspects of a physical system accurately. A theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature. Scientific evidence supports it, various groups of researchers have verified it multiple times, and it should describe all aspects of any system within its domain of applicability. Some theories include a model to help visualize the phenomena, as the kinetic theory of gases pictures a gas as atoms and molecules. Others do not: Newton’s theory of gravity needs no mental image, because we can observe the objects directly with our own senses. So a model can be part of a theory. A theory stands only if experiment verifies every one of its testable implications, while a model needs only to help within its limited situations.

exercises.prompt: If two different theories describe experimental observations equally well, can one be said to be more valid than the other (assuming both use accepted rules of logic)?

answer.solution: In the sense the text gives the word, no. A theory is valid when experiment has verified its testable implications and shown none of them false. If two theories account for every observation equally well, experiment has not yet told them apart. Scientists may still prefer one, for example the simpler one or the one that covers a wider domain, but that preference is a matter of convenience and elegance. Experiment alone makes a theory right or wrong. To decide between the two, find an implication on which they differ and perform that experiment; until then, both are valid within the observations made so far.

exercises.prompt: What determines the validity of a theory?

answer.solution: Experiment does. A theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, and experiments should verify each of its testable implications. When an experiment shows an implication to be false, scientists throw the theory out or modify it suitably, for example by limiting its domain of applicability. A theory earns its standing when various groups of researchers verify it, repeatedly. Even so, no one can know a theory with absolute certainty, since no one can perform every imaginable experiment, so physicists take every theory to be valid until they observe a counterexample.

exercises.prompt: Certain criteria must be satisfied if a measurement or observation is to be believed. Will the criteria necessarily be as strict for an expected result as for an unexpected result?

answer.solution: The standard of evidence is the same in principle. The cornerstone of discovering natural laws is observation, and science must describe the universe as it is, not as we imagine it to be. Al-Haytham’s lesson is that senses and predisposition can lead to poor conclusions, so a scientist trusts only objective evidence and stands ready to reject existing knowledge. In practice, scientists examine an unexpected result more closely. A good-quality, verifiable experiment that contradicts a well-established law means the law must change or fall, and no one takes that step until others have repeated and validated the experiment. An expected result agrees with what many experiments have already verified, so it carries less weight on its own. The extra scrutiny reflects how much a result would overturn, not a different rule. The real danger is the opposite one: believing an expected result too easily.

exercises.prompt: Can the validity of a model be limited, or must it be universally valid? How does this compare to the required validity of a theory or a law?

answer.solution: A model’s nature limits its validity. Experimental proof justifies a model, but it is accurate only under limited situations and describes only certain aspects of a physical system. The planetary model of the atom helps us picture atomic spectra, and no one expects it to be the whole truth about an atom. A theory must do more: it should describe all aspects of any system within its domain of applicability. A law is a concise and very general statement that repeated experiments support. Both a theory and a law must hold everywhere within their domain, and a single good-quality, verifiable experiment against them forces scientists to modify or overthrow them. Even a theory or a law has a domain, since classical physics is an excellent approximation only under stated conditions. The difference is that a model may be knowingly partial, while a theory or a law must hold throughout the range it claims.

exercises.prompt: Classical physics is a good approximation to modern physics under certain circumstances. What are they?

answer.solution: Three conditions must hold. Matter must move at speeds less than about 1% of the speed of light. The objects must be large enough to see with a microscope. Only weak gravitational fields, such as the field the Earth generates, may be involved. Because humans live under such circumstances, classical physics seems intuitively reasonable, and it describes the universe extremely accurately under a wide range of everyday circumstances.

exercises.prompt: When is it necessary to use relativistic quantum mechanics?

answer.solution: Relativistic quantum mechanics combines relativity and quantum mechanics, and you need it when both apply at once: for objects smaller than a microscope can show that travel at more than about 1% of the speed of light or feel a strong gravitational field, such as that near the Sun. It is the best universally applicable theory we have. Because of its mathematical complexity, physicists use it only when necessary and use the other theories whenever they give sufficiently accurate results.

exercises.prompt: Can classical physics be used to accurately describe a satellite moving at a speed of 7500 m/s? Explain why or why not.

answer.solution: Yes. Check the satellite against the three conditions. The speed of light is about $3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, so 7500 m/s is $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$ of it, which is 0.0025%, far below the 1% at which relativity must be used. A satellite is far larger than anything that needs a microscope to be seen, so quantum mechanics is not needed. The gravitational field it moves in is the Earth’s, which the text names as the example of a weak field. All three conditions are met, so classical physics describes the satellite’s motion accurately. Note that the GPS satellites the section mentions do carry small relativistic corrections, but only because they keep time to nanoseconds, which is the effect of time dilation the passage on GPS hints at; the motion itself is classical.
